\chapter{La cola y el carné}
\label{ch:es-turno}
\hlchaptermodality{451}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can get through a counter: queue, put my name on a list, show the right card, keep the right slip of paper, and follow a notice that says what will be checked and when.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la cola]{la cola — the queue}

\label{lesson:ES-C451-cola}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{esperar} and \textbf{la entrada}. Name what forms between the two.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la cola}
\textbf{la cola} — the queue, the line of people.

\emph{Hay mucha cola} — there's a long queue. \emph{Hacer cola} — to queue: \emph{llevo media hora haciendo cola}. \emph{Ponte a la cola} — get in line. \emph{El último de la cola} — the last person in the queue.

Spanish says \textbf{hacer} cola, never \emph{estar en} cola. You \emph{make} a queue by standing in it, which puts the work where it belongs.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two colas, and one of them is glue}]
There are three separate words spelled \textbf{cola} in Spanish, and none of them is related to the others:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the word} & \textbf{where it comes from} \\
\midrule
\textbf{la cola} — tail, queue & Latin \emph{cauda} \\
\textbf{la cola} — glue & Greek \emph{kólla} \\
\textbf{la cola} — the drink & a West African word for the nut \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{La cola del perro} is the dog's tail. \emph{Un bote de cola} is a pot of glue. \emph{Una cola} at a bar is the drink. Nothing but context separates them, and context always does: nobody queues in a tube and nobody glues at the entrance.

Words that collide like this are called homonyms, and Spanish has fewer of them than English because its spelling is so regular that unrelated words rarely arrive at the same shape. When they do, it is worth knowing, because a dictionary will list them as two entries and you might otherwise think you had missed a connection.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{cauda}, tail.

The jump from tail to queue is one picture: a line of people trailing behind something, the way a tail trails behind an animal. French made the same jump with \emph{queue}, which English then borrowed — and \emph{queue} is also from \emph{cauda}. So the English and Spanish words for a line of people are the same Latin word, arrived at independently.

The \emph{au} closing to \emph{o} is regular: \emph{causa} gave \emph{cosa}, \emph{paucum} gave \emph{poco}, \emph{taurum} gave \emph{toro}. The \textbf{l} is not. Spanish inherited the word through a spoken form \textbf{coda}, and the step from \emph{coda} to \emph{cola} is one nobody has a tidy rule for — which is worth saying, because most of the sound changes in this material do have one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item there's a long queue at the entrance
  \item I've been queuing for half an hour
  \item which verb goes with \emph{cola}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The queue? (\textbf{La cola}.) To queue? (\textbf{Hacer cola}.) What was a \emph{cauda}? (\textbf{A tail}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[apuntar]{apuntar — put it down}

\label{lesson:ES-C451-apuntar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el punto} and \textbf{la cola}. The first is inside the verb you are about to meet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: apuntar}
\textbf{apuntar} — to note down, to jot.

\emph{Apunta el número} — write the number down. \emph{Voy a apuntarlo} — I'll make a note of it.

And with \textbf{-se}, the meaning most useful at a counter: \textbf{apuntarse}, to put your name down, to sign up.

\emph{Me apunto a la excursión} — I'm putting my name down for the trip. \emph{¿Te apuntas?} — are you in? That last one is an invitation to anything at all, and it is the phrase you will hear when a group is deciding something.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: apuntar is not escribir}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you are doing} & \textbf{the verb} \\
\midrule
producing text & \textbf{escribir} \\
capturing something before it escapes & \textbf{apuntar} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You \emph{escribes} a letter, an essay, a message. You \emph{apuntas} a phone number, an address, a time somebody has said aloud. The difference is not length; it is purpose. \emph{Apuntar} is always about not losing the thing.

That is why \emph{apuntarse} means signing up: you are getting your name captured onto a list before the places run out.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{a-punt-ar}, built straight on \textbf{el punto}, and behind that Latin \textbf{punctum}, a prick — from \textbf{pungere}, to pierce.

So \emph{apuntar} is to put a point on something. All three of its senses are that one action: to note a thing down is to mark a point on paper, to \emph{apuntar} a weapon is to aim its point, and to \emph{apuntarse} is to put a point beside your own name.

The family is wide. A \textbf{puncture} is a piercing, a \textbf{punctual} person hits the point in time, and \textbf{puntiagudo} in Spanish is sharp-pointed. Every one of them has a small sharp thing in it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item write the number down
  \item I'm putting my name down for the trip
  \item why \emph{apuntar} and \emph{el punto} are the same word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To note down? (\textbf{Apuntar}.) To sign up? (\textbf{Apuntarse}.) What does \emph{¿te apuntas?} invite? (\textbf{Joining in with whatever is being planned}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el carné]{el carné — the card with your name on it}

\label{lesson:ES-C451-carne}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el documento} and \textbf{apuntarse}. You sign up, and then they hand you something.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el carné}
\textbf{el carné} — the card: an official one, with your name on it.

\emph{El carné de identidad} — the ID card. \emph{El carné de conducir} — the driving licence. \emph{El carné de la biblioteca} — the library card. \emph{El carné joven} — the youth discount card.

Plural \textbf{los carnés}. You will also see the French spelling \textbf{carnet}, which is common on forms and older signs.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: carné is not tarjeta}]
Two Spanish words land on English \textquotedblleft{}card\textquotedblright{}, and they divide the work cleanly:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the card} & \textbf{the word} \\
\midrule
proves who you are or what you may do & \textbf{el carné} \\
pays, greets, or carries an address & \textbf{la tarjeta} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{La tarjeta de crédito}, \emph{la tarjeta de cumpleaños}, \emph{la tarjeta de visita} — none of those could be a \emph{carné}. And a driving licence could never be a \emph{tarjeta}, however much plastic it is made of.

The test is whether somebody official issued it about \textbf{you}. If yes, it is a \emph{carné}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
French \textbf{carnet}, a small notebook — from Old French \emph{quernet}, and behind that Latin \textbf{quaternum}, a set of four.

Four what? Four sheets of paper folded together, which is how a small notebook was made. The same \emph{quaternum} gave Spanish \textbf{el cuaderno}, and the two words are the same object seen at different sizes: a \emph{cuaderno} stayed a notebook, while the French \emph{carnet} shrank to the single card you carry.

Latin \textbf{quattuor}, four, is behind both, and behind \emph{cuatro}, \emph{cuarto} and \emph{cuarenta}. A driving licence has four sheets of paper folded inside its history.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the ID card and the driving licence
  \item I'm signing up, so I need the library card
  \item which of \emph{carné} and \emph{tarjeta} would pay for something
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The ID card? (\textbf{El carné de identidad}.) The driving licence? (\textbf{El carné de conducir}.) What number is hiding in the word? (\textbf{Four} — \emph{quaternum}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mostrar]{mostrar — show it}

\label{lesson:ES-C451-mostrar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{ver} and \textbf{el carné}. Somebody at a desk wants to do the first to the second.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: mostrar}
\textbf{mostrar} — to show.

\begin{quote}
Es obligatorio \textbf{mostrar} el carné a la entrada.
\end{quote}

\emph{Muéstrame la lista} — show me the list. \emph{El gráfico muestra tres años} — the chart shows three years.

In speech Spaniards more often say \textbf{enseñar} for this — \emph{enséñame el carné}. \textbf{Mostrar} is what the sign says and what the form says, so it is a word you read more than you speak. Knowing which register a word belongs to is part of knowing the word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the o that breaks again}]
You have watched a stressed \textbf{o} turn into \textbf{ue} in \emph{la rueda}. Here it is inside a verb, doing exactly the same thing:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{stress on the stem} & \textbf{stress on the ending} \\
\midrule
m\textbf{ue}stro, m\textbf{ue}stras & mostr\textbf{a}mos \\
m\textbf{ue}stra, m\textbf{ue}stran & mostr\textbf{á}is \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The infinitive \emph{mostrar} has the plain \textbf{o} because the stress is on the \emph{-ar}. Push the stress back onto the stem and the vowel breaks.

So this verb is not irregular in any interesting sense. It is one vowel obeying one condition, and the same condition you used to explain a noun now explains a conjugation.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{monstrare}, to point out — from \textbf{monstrum}, and that is where it gets interesting.

A \emph{monstrum} was an omen: something strange that the gods had \textbf{shown} you as a warning. The horror came later, from the strangeness of the sign. So \textbf{mostrar} and \textbf{monstruo} are the same root, one keeping the showing and the other keeping the thing shown.

English has both halves as well, in \textbf{demonstrate} and \textbf{monster}, and the pair is a clean example of a root splitting into a neutral word and a frightening one while the idea inside stays the same: something put where you cannot miss it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item you must show your card at the entrance
  \item show me the list
  \item which form a friend would use instead
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To show? (\textbf{Mostrar}.) I show? (\textbf{Muestro} — stress on the stem.) What was a \emph{monstrum}? (\textbf{An omen, something shown as a warning}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el ticket]{el ticket — the receipt}

\label{lesson:ES-C451-ticket}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el billete} and \textbf{la entrada}. Neither of them is what the till prints.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el ticket}
\textbf{el ticket} — the receipt, the slip from the till.

\emph{¿Quiere el ticket?} — would you like the receipt? \emph{Guarde el ticket para cambios} — keep the receipt for exchanges. \emph{El ticket de la compra} — the shopping receipt.

Said \textbf{TI-ket}. Spanish also writes it \textbf{tique}, and the shorter \textbf{el recibo} covers the same ground in more formal use — on an invoice, or where money has changed hands between businesses.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three slips of paper, three words}]
English calls all of these a ticket. Spanish will not:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what it does} & \textbf{the word} \\
\midrule
carries you somewhere & \textbf{el billete} \\
gets you in & \textbf{la entrada} \\
proves you paid & \textbf{el ticket} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A train journey is \emph{un billete}. A concert is \emph{una entrada}. What the supermarket hands you is \emph{un ticket}, and asking for \emph{un billete} at a till would suggest you wanted a banknote, since \emph{billete} covers that too.

Sort them by the job rather than by the paper, and all three stay apart.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
This word has been around the houses.

Old French \textbf{estiquier} meant to stick — a Frankish word, Germanic in origin, the same family as English \emph{stick}. From it came \textbf{estiquet}, a little notice \emph{stuck} onto something: a label.

English borrowed \emph{estiquet} and wore it down to \textbf{ticket}, meanwhile narrowing it from any label to a paid-for slip. Spanish then borrowed the English word back, keeping the English spelling.

Spanish also kept the original French form separately, as \textbf{la etiqueta} — a label, and by extension the rules of polite behaviour, which were once literally the notices posted at court telling visitors how to behave. One Frankish word for sticking something on a surface, and it has ended up as a supermarket receipt and as the word \emph{etiquette}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item would you like the receipt?
  \item keep the receipt and show it at the desk
  \item which of the three words fits a concert
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The receipt? (\textbf{El ticket}.) The way in? (\textbf{La entrada}.) What did \emph{estiquier} mean? (\textbf{To stick} — it was a label.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[revisar]{revisar — look at it again}

\label{lesson:ES-C451-revisar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{ver} and \textbf{el aviso}. Both have the same Latin verb inside them, and so does the word coming next.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: revisar}
\textbf{revisar} — to check, to go over, to inspect.

\emph{Voy a revisar el ticket} — I'll check the receipt. \emph{Han revisado el coche} — they've serviced the car. \emph{Revisa las respuestas antes de entregar} — check your answers before handing it in.

Two nouns come with it: \textbf{la revisión}, the check-up or the service, and \textbf{el revisor}, the inspector who comes down the train.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: revisar is not mirar}]
Three verbs of looking, now sorted:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what happens} & \textbf{the verb} \\
\midrule
it arrives at your eyes & \textbf{ver} \\
you aim your eyes at it & \textbf{mirar} \\
you go over it for faults & \textbf{revisar} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Veo el ticket} — the receipt is in my field of vision. \emph{Miro el ticket} — I direct my attention at it. \emph{Reviso el ticket} — I am checking whether they charged me twice.

Only the third carries the idea of a verdict at the end. That is why a mechanic \emph{revisa} a car and a passenger merely \emph{mira} the timetable.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{re-vis-ar}: the prefix \emph{re-}, again, on the stem \emph{vis-} from Latin \textbf{videre}, to see, through its participle \emph{visus}.

So \emph{revisar} is to see again — the second look, which is the one where you find what the first look missed.

You have met this root twice already without the seeing being visible. \textbf{Ver} is \emph{videre} worn down to two letters. \textbf{El aviso} is \emph{a-vis-o}, a bringing to someone's sight. Add \emph{revisar} and you have three words from one Latin verb, each hiding it to a different degree. The English cousins run alongside: \textbf{vision}, \textbf{advise}, \textbf{revise}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I'll check the receipt
  \item check your answers before handing it in
  \item what \emph{ver}, \emph{aviso} and \emph{revisar} share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To check over? (\textbf{Revisar}.) The inspector on the train? (\textbf{El revisor}.) What does the \emph{re-} add? (\textbf{Again} — it is the second look.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(la cola, apuntar, el carné, mostrar …]{(la cola, apuntar, el carné, mostrar, el ticket, revisar) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R451-repaso-turno}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all six: \emph{the queue}, \emph{to note down}, \emph{the card}, \emph{to show}, \emph{the receipt}, \emph{to check}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which slip of paper}]
Four words now cover what English calls a card or a ticket. The sort is by job, not by material:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what it does} & \textbf{the word} \\
\midrule
says who you are & el carné \\
carries you somewhere & el billete \\
gets you in & la entrada \\
proves you paid & el ticket \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the left-hand column aloud and the right-hand one answers itself. Try to remember it as four pieces of plastic and paper and it will not, because three of them look identical.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two verbs you already half-owned}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{new verb} & \textbf{what it was built on} \\
\midrule
\textbf{apuntar} & \emph{el punto}, and behind it \emph{pungere}, to pierce \\
\textbf{revisar} & \emph{ver} and \emph{el aviso}, and behind them \emph{videre} \\
\textbf{mostrar} & \emph{monstrum}, an omen — something shown \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Revisar} is the clearest case in the chapter. You have been saying \textbf{ver} since the beginning and \textbf{el aviso} for many chapters, without either one looking like Latin \emph{videre}. The third member makes the family visible, and now all three are cheaper to hold than any one of them was alone.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item there's a queue, so put your name down first
  \item you have to show your card at the entrance
  \item which verb means going over something for faults
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
All six again, in Spanish, without looking. Then one sentence that gets you from the back of a queue to a receipt in your hand.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(en el mostrador) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C451-sintesis-turno}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el carné} and \textbf{el ticket}. The notice below asks for both, at different moments.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
A notice above the counter at a leisure centre. Read it, then answer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{CAMBIOS Y DEVOLUCIONES}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
1. Haga \textbf{cola} en la ventanilla 2. No se atiende sin turno.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
2. \textbf{Muestre} el \textbf{carné} de socio y el \textbf{ticket} de compra.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
3. Si no tiene el ticket, \textbf{apúntese} en la lista y le llamamos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
4. \textbf{Revisamos} cada caso en 48 horas.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two things you must have with you
  \item what to do if you have lost the receipt
  \item how long the decision takes
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
The notice asks for two pieces of plastic and the words are not interchangeable. The \textbf{carné de socio} says who you are; the \textbf{ticket} says you paid. Lose the first and they cannot identify you; lose the second and they cannot see what you bought. So step three deals only with the missing ticket, and identity is still required.

Then look at the verbs. \textbf{Muestre}, \textbf{apúntese}, \textbf{haga} are all \emph{usted} commands — the register of any counter in Spain. \textbf{Apúntese} carries its pronoun on the end and takes a written accent to hold the stress where it was in \emph{apunte}; without the mark you would read \emph{apuntese} with the stress in the wrong place.

\textbf{Revisamos} breaks the pattern deliberately. The first three lines tell you what to do; the fourth says what \emph{we} do. Moving to \emph{nosotros} at the end is how a notice stops giving orders and starts making a promise.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four numbered lines for a counter notice: tell people to queue, to show a card, to keep the receipt, and say that you check each case within two days.

Then check yourself: did you use the \emph{usted} command for the instructions and switch to \emph{nosotros} for what the office does?
\end{tcolorbox}
